lesson.title: Expressions: The Building Blocks That Produce a Value
lesson.summary: An expression is any piece of Python code that evaluates down to a single value, built from literals, variables, and operators, and expressions are the raw material every statement in a program is assembled from.
lesson.body:
An expression is anything Python can reduce to one value. The simplest expressions are a bare literal, like the number 5, or a bare variable name, like x, since both of those already have a value on their own with nothing left to compute. Expressions become more interesting when operators combine several pieces together, as in x + 5 * 2, which is still a single expression because the whole thing eventually reduces to one number.

Expressions rely directly on Arithmetic Operators to combine values and on the ordering rules from Operator Precedence to decide which operation happens first when more than one operator appears. Trace a compound example carefully. Suppose x = 4, and consider the expression (x + 3) * 2 - x ** 2. Parentheses are evaluated first: x + 3 becomes 4 + 3, which is 7. Next, exponentiation outranks the remaining operators, so x ** 2 becomes 4 ** 2, which is 16. The expression is now effectively 7 * 2 - 16. Multiplication runs before subtraction, so 7 * 2 becomes 14. The final step is 14 - 16, which evaluates to negative 2. No matter how many operators and sub-parts an expression contains, Python always works it down to exactly one final value, in this case -2.

Expressions connect directly to Variable Assignment: the entire right-hand side of any assignment statement is an expression, and Python always evaluates it completely to a single value before that value gets stored under the name on the left. In a statement like result = (x + 3) * 2 - x ** 2, the right side is evaluated first, all the way down to -2, and only after that final value exists does the assignment actually happen, storing -2 in result.

Expressions can be as small as a single number or as elaborate as a deeply nested combination of operators, but the defining feature is always the same: given enough information, Python can compute exactly one value from it. This is different from a full instruction telling Python to do something, which is the idea covered next under Statements; an expression by itself just has a value, it does not necessarily do anything with that value until it is placed inside a statement.

Once expressions click as has a value rather than does something, they turn out to be everywhere: inside the parentheses of a print() call, inside the curly braces of an f-string, and later inside the conditions that control loops and branching decisions. Recognizing a chunk of code as an expression, and being able to trace what value it reduces to, is one of the most transferable skills in learning to read and predict what any piece of Python will actually do.

It is worth noticing that not every expression involves arithmetic at all. A string like "hello" is already a complete expression on its own, as is a concatenation like first + " " + last or a repetition like "-" * 20; each of those reduces to a single string value using the exact same has a value logic that governs numeric expressions like (x + 3) * 2 - x ** 2. The type of value an expression produces can differ, a number, a string, or later a boolean, but the underlying idea that the expression is evaluated down to one value stays consistent across every type Python supports.
